claims.text: In situ nitrogen-plasma treatment at 400–500°C will form an approximately 50 nm ZrN layer at the zirconium-alloy/Cr interface.
The resulting ZrN interlayer will be coherent.
ZrN is chemically inert under the proposed service and accident environments.
An ultrathin interfacial layer can function as a diffusion barrier at elevated temperature.
The approximately 50 nm ZrN layer will inhibit Cr and Zr interdiffusion at elevated temperatures.
Suppressing Cr–Zr interdiffusion will maintain the integrity of the Cr coating.
The ZrN interlayer will prevent premature Cr-coating failure during accident-relevant high-temperature steam exposure.
The ZrN-modified coating will retain protective performance during normal subcritical-water operation.
The proposed benefit will persist during steam exposure up to approximately 800–900°C for about 30 minutes.
The proposed benefit is expected to persist during repeated thermal cycling.
Directly Cr-coated zirconium-alloy cladding is prone to premature failure from Cr–Zr interdiffusion around 800–900°C.
Relative to the directly Cr-coated baseline, the ZrN-modified system will significantly reduce Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Relative to the baseline, the ZrN-modified system will better preserve structural integrity and mechanical adhesion after high-temperature steam exposure.
The long-term stability of the approximately 50 nm ZrN layer under prolonged cyclic thermal stress and extended steam exposure is uncertain.
A controlled comparison at 850°C in steam for 30 minutes can discriminate between the ZrN-modified coating and the unmodified Cr-coated baseline.
Similar interdiffusion, interfacial-phase formation, or adhesion degradation in modified and baseline samples would falsify the hypothesis.
